# VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement

Ruotian Peng  Yuanyi Ren  Shuaiqi Liu  Xin Guo Affiliation: Zhejiang
University    Affiliation: Westlake University    Affiliation: Alibaba
Token Hub, Alibaba Group       Fang Zhu  Yangyi Huang Affiliation: South
China University of Technology    Affiliation: The Chinese University of
Hong Kong^(\*)Equal contribution    ^(†)Corresponding author    Yue
Wu  Zheng Wang  Yandong Wen  Zhihang Fu Affiliation: Westlake
University    Affiliation: Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group   

###### Abstract

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system
bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference.
We refer to the agents’ capability to jointly optimize training data,
the trainer, and the inference harness as _cross-component co-design_.
We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this
capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software
engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within
each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system
under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they
iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select
and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To
prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data
isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network
restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that
frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For
example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent
system’s performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the
human-developed instruct model’s 55.4%. However, there is still room to
improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer,
and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that
VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI,
deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent
systems. Code and data are available at
[https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTraining-Bench](https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTraining-Bench).

## 1 Introduction

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), increasingly studied as a path toward
autonomous AI development, requires agents to diagnose performance
bottlenecks and propose and validate modifications to an agent
system ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). These modifications may involve training data, the
trainer, and the inference harness, with their effectiveness depending
on how these components are configured together ([Ursekar et al.,
2026](#bib.bib21)). For example, the harness controls what an agent
observes and can do, steering its exploration and thus the trajectories
the model learns from; conversely, the model’s capabilities determine
what the harness must provide ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib8); [Chen et
al., 2026d](#bib.bib17)). Agents must therefore trace failures to their
sources and coordinate changes across training and inference. We refer
to this capability as _cross-component co-design_.

Assessing cross-component co-design thus calls for settings in which
agents themselves determine which components to modify and how to
coordinate these modifications as the system evolves. To the best of our
knowledge, few benchmarks directly assess this capability. MLE-Bench and
RE-Bench evaluate research agents on diverse machine learning
engineering and research tasks, focusing on task-specific research
outcomes. More directly related RSI benchmarks often evaluate
single-component improvement. RSIBench-Data ([Meng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)), AI4AI-Bench ([Chi et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)), and
HarnessOpt-Bench ([Ursekar et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)) focus on data
strategies, training algorithms, and inference harnesses, respectively;
each MLS-Bench task specifies one ML component to improve ([Lyu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)). These benchmarks evaluate improvements within
predefined component scopes. PostTrainBench ([Rank et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20)) and Agent² RL-Bench ([Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib23)) broaden this scope to data construction and
post-training procedures. Simply broadening the editable scope also
raises evaluation risks: PostTrainBench reports reward hacking,
including research agents training on test data ([Rank et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20)). Even these multi-component benchmarks remain focused
on training-side optimization, leaving the iterative selection and
coordination of changes across training and inference within the same
evolving target system unexplored.

We introduce VibeTraining-Bench to evaluate cross-component co-design
through five tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering,
multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. In each task, an agent
receives an initial agent system comprising a base model, open-source
training data, a trainer with algorithm code and initial scripts, and an
inference harness. The agent must improve this system within a fixed
resource budget, and the agent it finally submits is then scored on
hidden test instances. During a run, validation scores and execution
trajectories help the agent trace failures to their sources and assess
successive revisions. The benchmark also allows the agent to choose
where to intervene and coordinate changes across components. Training
data and the trainer are editable in every task, as is the inference
harness unless the task’s evaluation prescribes a particular harness.
These design choices, however, also widen the opportunities for reward
hacking, so VibeTraining-Bench further enforces three safeguards, namely
data isolation, container isolation, and network restrictions.
Specifically, test data remain inaccessible throughout the research
phase; research and grading run in separate containers, preventing
research agents from modifying grader code or evaluation data; and
research environments strictly restrict external network access.

Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially
improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified,
GPT-6-Astra coordinates training and harness changes, raising the target
agent system’s performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the
human-developed instruct model’s 55.4%. However, research agents explore
the improvable system components unevenly. Analysis of research
trajectories shows that agents primarily focus on lightweight
refinements, such as data filtering and training hyperparameter tuning.
They less frequently explore changes to the underlying training
algorithms or coordinated modifications across training data, the
trainer, and the inference harness. There is still room for improvement
in research agents’ cross-component co-design capability and iterative
refinement toward achieving cumulative performance gains.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

- •
  We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse tasks
  for evaluating cross-component co-design of target agent systems. Its
  improvement scope encompasses training data, the trainer, and the
  inference harness.
- •
  We develop a reliable execution platform to guarantee evaluation
  integrity. To prevent research agents from reward hacking, our
  platform implements three levels of safeguards by isolating test data,
  separating research and grading containers, and restricting external
  network access.
- •
  We evaluate frontier research agents through test performance,
  research trajectories, and component ablations. Research agents
  substantially improve target agent systems, in some cases approaching
  the performance of the system with human post-training. Our
  experimental analysis reveals that research agents built upon frontier
  models and harnesses still exhibit limitations on these tasks,
  indicating substantial room for further improvement.

Trajectory feedback requires task-level traces or diagnostics, and
iterative revision requires repeated propose–evaluate–revise cycles.
Joint requires coordinated changes to training data, the trainer, and
the inference harness within one task. Dev/test isolation keeps the
final test inaccessible during development; train/eval isolation
separates training, serving, and evaluation services.

#### Self-evolving language models and agents.

Self-improving agent systems expose several non-exclusive intervention
surfaces: training data, trainer, and inference-time harnesses. On the
data front, prior work improves models through automated experience
generation, student-feedback loops, and self-synthesized
trajectories ([Zweiger et al., 2026](#bib.bib19); [Huang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib1); [Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)). On the trainer
front, recent methods leverage LLMs to discover novel optimization
objectives and adaptive reinforcement learning strategies ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Fang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)). On the inference
front, self-evolving agent frameworks optimize inference harnesses by
tuning prompts, tool interfaces, and runtime control flow, thereby
enhancing performance under frozen model weights ([Yin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). More recently, work
has begun to explore multi-component coupling. For example, [Chen et al.
(2026b)](#bib.bib7) reuse inference rollouts for training, while [Chen
et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib8) co-evolve harness and model weights;
nevertheless, these interactions follow static, predefined pathways.
Taken together, these efforts reflect an emerging shift toward coupled
system-level optimization. VibeTraining-Bench advances this paradigm to
an open-ended setting, evaluating whether research agents can
autonomously decide where and how to coordinate improvements across
data, trainer, and inference harnesses without a prescribed recipe.

#### Benchmarks for autonomous ML research and recursive self-improvement.

Existing benchmarks evaluate autonomous ML research across diverse axes,
including engineering, experimentation, replication, and algorithmic
discovery ([Huang et al., 2023](#bib.bib9); [Wijk et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib11); [Starace et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Lyu et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)). Within the context
of recursive self-improvement (RSI), existing benchmarks differ
primarily in the scope of system components exposed to the agent. To
ensure attribution clarity, most prior works isolate a single component:
Curation-Bench ([Kang et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)) and
RSIBench-Data ([Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)) focus on data curation;
AI4AI-Bench ([Chi et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)) targets training
algorithms, while HarnessOpt-Bench ([Ursekar et al., 2026](#bib.bib21))
and Evo-Bench ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib24)) optimize inference
scaffolding around fixed model weights. PostTrainBench and Agent²
RL-Bench broaden this scope to data construction and training-procedure
design, yet keep the deployed inference harness outside the optimization
loop ([Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib20); [Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib23)).
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
summarizes these protocol differences across the research loop, editable
components, and evaluation isolation. VibeTraining-Bench bridges this
gap by enabling cross-component co-design, placing training data, the
trainer, and the inference harness jointly under research agent control.
Crucially, because expanding the editable space naturally heightens the
risk of reward hacking ([Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)), our protocol
strictly isolates the research agent’s workspace from the grading
service, preventing test-set leakage during iterative improvement.

## 3 VibeTraining-Bench

![Refer to caption](2610.26342v2/VibeTrain-Bench_Main_Figure2.png)

Figure 1: Overview of VibeTraining-Bench. The benchmark assesses a
research agent’s capacity for systemic co-design across three
interdependent components: training data, the trainer, and the inference
harness. (Left) Research agents initialize from domain-specific data
sources and task-specific resource budgets shared across research-agent
configurations. (Center) Within the autonomous loop, research agents
iteratively orchestrate component modifications using validation signals
until budget exhaustion. (Right) Strict architectural decoupling
isolates the optimization workspace from the grading server to prevent
reward hacking. Only the visible validation set provides feedback; the
hidden test set remains inaccessible until independent test evaluation
of the selected system.

### 3.1 Overview and Task Formulation

VibeTraining-Bench evaluates whether a research agent can improve a
target agent system by iteratively selecting and coordinating changes to
its training data, trainer, and, where editable, inference harness. Each
task defines the permitted components and a fixed resource budget.
Within this space, the agent uses validation feedback to decide what to
modify next and which candidate target agent system to retain. Its
objective is to select an agent system that outperforms the initial
agent system on hidden test problems outside the research loop.

We formalize this process as follows: Each task supplies a base model
$`M_{0}`$, initial training data an trainer, an inference harness
$`H_{0}`$, and a resource budget $`\mathcal{B}`$. The initial target
agent system is $`P_{0}=(M_{0},H_{0})`$, and the research agent receives
its validation score and execution trajectories before making any
modifications. At research iteration $`t`$, the research agent may
modify the training data $`D_{t}`$, trainer $`T_{t}`$, or harness
$`H_{t}`$ within the task’s editable space. The trainer includes the
training algorithm and its configuration. The candidate target agent
system is $`P_{t}=(M_{t},H_{t})`$, where $`M_{t}`$ may be newly trained,
constructed by merging existing models, or reused from an earlier
iteration. Validation returns a score and per-task execution
trajectories on the requested validation tasks, which guide subsequent
iterations within the resource budget. Finally, the research agent
selects one candidate target agent system as $`P^{\star}`$ using
information available during research. An isolated grader evaluates this
system on hidden test problems disjoint from the validation problems. We
measure improvement over the initial target agent system as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\Delta_{\mathrm{test}}=\operatorname{Eval}_{\mathrm{test}}(P^{\star})-\operatorname{Eval}_{\mathrm{test}}(P_{0}).
``` |  | (1) |

The test result measures the selected target agent system’s improvement,
while the recorded attempts show which components the research agent
chose to modify.

### 3.2 Benchmark Suite

Task scope. We instantiate the proposed cross-component co-design
formulation across five target environments within VibeTraining-Bench,
spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use,
and mathematical reasoning. As summarized in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Benchmark Suite ‣ 3 VibeTraining-Bench ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement"),
these benchmarks present heterogeneous interaction paradigms under a
shared iterative improvement framework. Specifically, Terminal-Bench 2.1
and SWE-bench Verified require long-horizon execution grounded in
operating systems and codebases; $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench and Toolathlon
demand stateful tool utilization over multi-turn dialogues; and AIME
evaluates mathematical reasoning without external tool execution.
Consequently, this diversity in task formulations allows us to examine
whether research agents adapt their orchestration strategies across
heterogeneous operational contexts.

[TABLE]

Table 2: Task composition of VibeTraining-Bench. The editable space
indicates whether the research agent may modify training data ($`D`$),
the trainer ($`T`$), and the inference harness ($`H`$).

Editable components. We systematically define the editable space of each
target agent system over three components: the training data, the
trainer, and the inference harness. Across all tasks, research agents
can access the pre-provisioned data repositories and training framework
code to modify training data, algorithms, and hyperparameters. Whether
the inference harness is editable depends on the task. For
Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench Verified, the inference harness
controls how the target agent system interacts with terminal and
codebase environments, including execution loops, command-line
invocations, and memory management. We therefore make the harness
editable in these two tasks to support comprehensive cross-component
co-design of training data, the trainer, and inference-time behavior
within the same target agent system. For $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench and
Toolathlon, the benchmark-provided execution adapters remain fixed. AIME
also fixes its evaluation interface and decoding settings. These three
tasks therefore expose training data and the trainer, but not the
inference harness, for modification.

### 3.3 Validation and Isolated Grading

Grading boundary. To prevent reward hacking, VibeTraining-Bench enforces
three safeguards: data isolation, container isolation, and network
restrictions. Test tasks and test-derived feedback remain inaccessible
throughout the research loop. The research agent’s workspace and the
grading service run in separate containers, preventing the research
agent from modifying grader code or evaluation data. External network
access is blocked in the research sandbox. Research agents request
validation through a controlled interface. For each request, the
independent grader evaluates the candidate target agent system
$`P_{t}`$, whose modifications are restricted to the task-permitted
components described in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Benchmark Suite ‣ 3 VibeTraining-Bench ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement").
It returns feedback $`f_{t}`$ consisting of the validation score and
per-task execution trajectories for the validation tasks. The research
agent can use this feedback to guide subsequent modifications.

Termination and final assessment. When the research phase ends, the
research agent selects one candidate target agent system as
$`P^{\star}`$ using the information available during research. It
submits $`P^{\star}`$ to the independent grading service, which
evaluates it exactly once on the test partition. Unlike iterative
validation, this final assessment provides no feedback to the research
agent for further revision. We report the benchmark test score of
$`P^{\star}`$.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Benchmark Suite ‣ 3 VibeTraining-Bench ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
summarizes the validation and test tasks, with additional partition
details in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Task Partitions and Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Details ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement").

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setup

We evaluate six research-agent configurations, each pairing an LLM with
a coding framework. GPT-5.6-Sol and GPT-6-Astra use Codex at xhigh
reasoning effort; Kimi-K3, Qwen-3.8-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.2
use Claude Code. Each research-agent run has access to eight NVIDIA A100
GPUs. Within each task, all configurations start from Qwen3.5-9B-Base
and the same initial training data
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Initial Training Data ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Details ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")),
and share the target-task interface, editable components, and
task-specific resource budget
(Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Benchmark Suite ‣ 3 VibeTraining-Bench ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
Each task provides validation tasks for iterative research and test
tasks for final evaluation. Terminal-Bench 2.1 uses OpenThoughts-TBLite
for validation, Toolathlon uses ToolGym, and AIME uses AIME 2025.
SWE-bench Verified and $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench use disjoint validation and
test partitions of their respective benchmarks. The isolated grader
evaluates the system on the hidden test using the task-specific scoring
and decoding settings. We report its benchmark-native test score. More
details are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional Experimental Details ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement").

### 4.2 Main Results

Figure 2: Mean generated tokens and macro-averaged final performance
across five benchmarks. Dashed line marks the initial system score.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
reports test scores for the selected target agent systems, each
comprising a selected model checkpoint and a task-specific inference
harness. The average across the five tasks is 22.7% for the initial
target agent systems and ranges from 31.1% to 38.3% across the six
research-agent configurations, with Kimi-K3 highest. The largest gain
over the initial target agent system occurs on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench, where
Kimi-K3 raises the score from 20.3% to 52.1%. On SWE-bench Verified,
GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system’s performance from 32.9% to
53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model’s 55.4%. On
Terminal-Bench 2.1, Kimi-K3 raises the score from 8.9% to 22.4%, while
GPT-5.6-Sol remains at 8.9%. These results show that large gains are
possible, but improvement is not guaranteed in every run.

The leader changes across tasks. GPT-6-Astra scores highest on SWE-bench
Verified (53.7%), Kimi-K3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (22.4%) and
$`\tau^{3}`$-Bench (52.1%), DeepSeek-V4-Pro on Toolathlon (12.5%), and
GLM-5.2 on AIME 2026 (63.3%). Among the four configurations using Claude
Code, the gap between the highest and lowest scores ranges from 5.7
percentage points on Toolathlon to 15.9 points on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench. No
research-agent configuration leads across all five tasks. Research time
alone does not account for these outcomes. Across the five tasks,
Qwen-3.8-Max uses 81.8 hours, 8.8 hours more than Kimi-K3, but scores
lower on four tasks. The following analyses examine validation
trajectories, resource use, and component choices behind the final
scores.

### 4.3 Validation Dynamics and Generalization

Figure 3: Each point represents a completed validation evaluation,
ordered chronologically within each run. Repeated evaluations of the
same candidate are shown separately.

As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Validation Dynamics and Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement"),
the best validation performance does not consistently translate into the
best test performance. GPT-5.6-Sol achieves an AIME validation score of
59.2%, yet scores 50.8% on the AIME 2026 test set, below GLM-5.2’s
63.3%. GPT-6-Astra leads validation on Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench
Verified, and $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench, and ties for the highest Toolathlon
validation score. However, it does not consistently lead on the
corresponding test sets. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it scores 13.5%,
compared with Kimi-K3’s leading score of 22.4%. On $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench,
Kimi-K3 also achieves the highest test score at 52.1%, ahead of
GPT-6-Astra’s 49.7%. These results show that validation leadership does
not reliably predict test leadership. The validation search is also
non-monotonic: later attempts do not necessarily improve on earlier
candidates. DeepSeek-V4-Pro’s later AIME validation scores fall to zero,
while GPT-6-Astra’s SWE-bench Verified validation score declines after
its peak and its later Toolathlon attempts fail to improve on an early
candidate.

### 4.4 Token usage analysis

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
compares each research agent’s mean generated tokens per run with its
macro-averaged test score across the five benchmarks. The target systems
produced by each of the six research agents achieve an average score
above the initial systems’ 22.7% across the five benchmarks. But higher
token usage does not correspond to higher performance. GLM-5.2 uses the
fewest tokens (91.1K per run), while Kimi-K3 achieves the highest score
(38.3%) with 173.2K tokens. These two agents form the observed Pareto
frontier. Qwen-3.8-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GPT-5.6-Sol use more tokens
than Kimi-K3 while scoring lower. GPT-6-Astra achieves the
second-highest average score at 37.1%, but uses by far the most
generated tokens. It therefore does not change the observed Pareto
frontier formed by GLM-5.2 and Kimi-K3.

Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.5 Component Ablations ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
shows that harness-only editing improves the initial target agent system
on SWE-bench Verified but not on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On SWE-bench
Verified, the harness-only run raises the test score from 32.9% to
38.0%. Kimi-K3’s unrestricted run reaches 51.7% without editing the
harness, leaving this harness-based direction unexplored. On
Terminal-Bench 2.1, the harness-only run scores 8.9%, matching the
initial agent system. The data-and-trainer-only run reaches 13.5%, while
the unrestricted run also edits the harness and reaches 22.4%.

## 5 Agent Behavior Analysis

### 5.1 Research Effort Allocation Across Components

We define a design as a distinct modification to the training data,
trainer, or inference harness that the research agent implements during
a run. Repeated submissions of an unchanged candidate count as one
design. A design that modifies multiple components contributes to the
count for each affected component.
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Research Effort Allocation Across Components ‣ 5 Agent Behavior Analysis ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
reports the number of designs involving each component. Every research
agent modifies data in each task, but the emphasis varies. On AIME 2026,
GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6-Sol, and GLM-5.2 propose more trainer than data
designs, whereas on SWE-bench Verified every research agent except
GPT-6-Astra proposes more data designs. Preferences also differ across
research agents: Qwen-3.8-Max favors data in all five tasks, while
GPT-6-Astra favors the trainer in four of five. GPT-5.6-Sol shifts from
trainer-focused designs on AIME 2026 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 to
data-focused designs on SWE-bench Verified. Some designs modify multiple
components: all seven of GPT-5.6-Sol’s $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench designs modify
both training data and the trainer. Harness exploration varies within
the two tasks that permit it. On SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra
proposes four harness designs, GPT-5.6-Sol proposes two, and Kimi-K3
proposes none. These patterns show that research agents use the editable
space differently, both in which components they prioritize and in
whether they change components together.

Figure 4: Number of designs involving training data, the trainer, and
the inference harness. A design may involve multiple components. Numbers
below the research-agent labels indicate the total number of distinct
designs in each run.

### 5.2 Component Pattern Analysis

Data strategies. Two patterns recur in how research agents construct
training data. (1) Trajectory filtering. Research agents use similar
filtering procedures: retaining successful trajectories, imposing length
limits, deduplicating prompts, and removing repetitive execution loops.
On SWE-bench Verified, Qwen-3.8-Max and GPT-5.6-Sol remove trajectories
with excessive repeated commands. On Toolathlon, Kimi-K3 filters
trajectories with repeated tool calls. (2) Format alignment. Research
agents adapt training examples to the inference harness and evaluation
settings. On SWE-bench Verified, Kimi-K3 reformats training prompts to
match the inference harness. Qwen-3.8-Max revises tool-call formatting
on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench, while GPT-6-Astra selects AIME examples with
complete \boxed{} answers.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Trainer strategies. All six research agents use supervised fine-tuning
(SFT). Their trainer modifications focus on hyperparameters, loss
calculation, and model merging. (1) Training settings. Most
modifications adjust training hyperparameters. GLM-5.2 tests additional
epochs on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench, but validation performance declines.
GPT-5.6-Sol tests multiple learning rates on Terminal-Bench, while
GPT-6-Astra reduces the training batch size on SWE-bench Verified.
Qwen-3.8-Max reduces the pipeline parallel size on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench to
accelerate training. (2) Loss calculation. On AIME, GPT-5.6-Sol
increases the loss weight on \</think\> to encourage shorter outputs,
improving the validation score from 60/120 to 71/120 with the same
examples. GPT-6-Astra adds supervision on valid historical assistant
turns in $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench examples to obtain more training targets.
(3) Model merging. On AIME, Kimi-K3 compares two-model and three-model
merges and selects the two-model merge after it scores higher on
validation. DeepSeek-V4-Pro tests different interpolation coefficients
on Terminal-Bench to select the final model weights. GPT-6-Astra merges
two trained models on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench, achieving the highest
validation score in its run.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Case study of GPT-6-Astra’s research trajectory on SWE-bench
Verified. Selected decisions illustrate how validation feedback guides
changes to training data, the trainer, and the inference harness.
Ellipses indicate omitted decisions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Harness strategies. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1,
harness modifications focus on execution control and parsing recovery.
(1) Execution control. GPT-5.6-Sol adds guards against repeated commands
and unchanged patches on SWE-bench Verified, reducing median API calls
from 163 to 96.5 in a paired 30-task comparison. On Terminal-Bench 2.1,
Kimi-K3 adds a completion checklist that prompts the target agent to
verify task requirements before declaring completion. (2) Output
recovery. Research agents modify output parsers to recover from
malformed responses. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSeek-V4-Pro adds
automatic repairs for escaping issues, missing colons, truncated
outputs, and trailing commas. GPT-6-Astra also adds automatic repair of
invalid escape sequences and revises JSON extraction logic to better
identify structured responses.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.3 Case Study

The GPT-6-Astra run on SWE-bench Verified illustrates how validation
feedback guides changes to training data, the trainer, and the inference
harness
(Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Component Pattern Analysis ‣ 5 Agent Behavior Analysis ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
After the research agent trains the model on demonstrations for 1,536
issues from Orchard, a software-repair training dataset, execution
traces reveal a Python interpreter mismatch. The research agent revises
the harness to use the repository’s existing Python environment while
preserving the agent’s own interpreter. With model weights fixed, this
revision increases the number of validation tasks solved from 45 to 55.
The agent also expands training to 4,096 issues and evaluates the
resulting checkpoints with the revised harness. The step-128 and
step-256 checkpoints solve 54 and 68 of the validation tasks,
respectively. The agent selects the step-256 model with the revised
harness, achieving 53.7% on the hidden test.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark designed to
evaluate research agents’ cross-component co-design capabilities across
diverse domains. In each task, a research agent begins with an initial
target agent system and iteratively modifies the training data, the
trainer, and the task-specific inference harness. Finally, the research
agent selects and submits a final agent system for evaluation on test
tasks. We develop a reliable execution platform to guarantee evaluation
integrity. To prevent research agents from reward hacking, our platform
implements three levels of safeguards by isolating test data, separating
research and grading containers, and restricting external network
access. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents can
substantially improve target agent systems, in some cases approaching
the performance of the system with human post-training. However, an
in-depth analysis of research agents’ trajectories and component
ablation experiments reveals that these research agents still exhibit
limitations. There is still room to improve their ability to co-design
and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative
performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a
unified platform for the community to develop more reliable and
effective research agents for recursive self-improvement.

## AI Use Statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to draft and polish portions
of the manuscript, and to improve clarity, grammar, and readability. We
did not use generative AI tools for the research tasks requiring
disclosure under the ICLR policy. All AI-assisted text was reviewed and
edited by the authors, who take responsibility for the final content of
this work, including all claims and results.

## Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies

### A.1 Case Study: Kimi-K3 on Terminal-Bench

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: Kimi-K3 on Terminal-Bench. The selected system combines the
expanded data mixture with the revised harness.

Kimi-K3 first trains the model to use the terminal interaction format,
then uses validation failures to target recovery and completion behavior
(Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.1 Case Study: Kimi-K3 on Terminal-Bench ‣ Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
Recovery-focused continuation raises solves from 4/50 to 10/50. A
fixed-weight harness revision leaves that total unchanged, although its
completion checklist is followed by resumed commands in 28 of 66
completion events. Kimi-K3 then expands demonstrations per task and
selects the resulting model with the revised harness at 12/50.

### A.2 Case Study: Qwen-3.8-Max on Terminal-Bench

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7: Qwen-3.8-Max on Terminal-Bench. The data curriculum changes
while the training recipe and harness remain fixed.

Qwen-3.8-Max responds to premature completion and long loops by changing
the demonstrated behavior
(Figure [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.2 Case Study: Qwen-3.8-Max on Terminal-Bench ‣ Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
It replaces a broad keyword heuristic with a filter for explicit tests,
output checks, and parsing commands, then gives these examples more
curriculum weight and limits long TerminalTraj records. Both models
train afresh from the same base on 16,000 examples with the same
250-step recipe and harness. The revised curriculum is selected after
validation changes from 5/50 to 9/50.

### A.3 Case Study: GPT-5.6-Sol on Terminal-Bench

GPT-5.6-Sol's validation failures expose a mismatch between intended and
executed training
(Figure [8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ A.3 Case Study: GPT-5.6-Sol on Terminal-Bench ‣ Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
In Decisions 2, 4, and 6, the agent intends to continue training from a
trained checkpoint but instead initializes the model randomly: the
loader receives an iteration directory rather than its parent checkpoint
root. Correcting the path preserves the data, learning rate, and harness
of the preceding comparison and raises validation from 0/50 to 12/50.
Later checkpoint, data, and training branches do not exceed this result;
GPT-5.6-Sol retains the correctly initialized continuation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: GPT-5.6-Sol on Terminal-Bench. Decisions 6 and 7 hold data,
learning rate, and harness fixed while correcting initialization.

### A.4 Case Study: GLM-5.2 on Terminal-Bench

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 9: GLM-5.2 on Terminal-Bench. Data expansion fails to improve on
the first selected model–harness pair.

GLM-5.2 tests data expansion after aligning demonstrations and terminal
instructions
(Figure [9](#A1.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ A.4 Case Study: GLM-5.2 on Terminal-Bench ‣ Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
Increasing the mixture from 6,315 to 12,000 records leaves validation at
8/50; expanding to 15,000 records with a new seed lowers it to 5/50. The
one-epoch recipe and harness are retained throughout these expansions.
GLM-5.2 selects the first model. The larger step counts follow the
larger datasets rather than an independent change to the learning
recipe.

### A.5 Case Study: DeepSeek-V4-Pro on Terminal-Bench

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 10: DeepSeek-V4-Pro on Terminal-Bench. Two-model merging and
three-checkpoint averaging are Trainer interventions.

DeepSeek-V4-Pro moves from data and execution repairs to model merging
(Figure [10](#A1.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ A.5 Case Study: DeepSeek-V4-Pro on Terminal-Bench ‣ Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
Its parser-only attempt, omitted as Decision 2, lowers validation from
10/50 to 5/50. Broader training and revised parser feedback restore
10/50. DeepSeek-V4-Pro then tests whether weight mixtures combine the
two trained models' capabilities. It selects the 0.25/0.75 mixture at
12/50; averaging the weights of three checkpoints and testing nearby
mixture coefficients yield lower validation scores. Six subsequent
submissions reuse the selected weights and harness, including one failed
job, and do not add designs.

### A.6 Case Study: GPT-6-Astra on Terminal-Bench

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 11: GPT-6-Astra on Terminal-Bench. The selected Data + Trainer
intervention lies between two fixed-weight Harness comparisons.

GPT-6-Astra alternates fixed-weight harness comparisons with changes to
supervision and training
(Figure [11](#A1.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ A.6 Case Study: GPT-6-Astra on Terminal-Bench ‣ Appendix A Terminal-Bench Case Studies ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")).
The first harness revision leaves the solved count at five. Recovery and
completion supervision, combined with continuation from the first model,
raises validation to 13/50. Longer-action training lowers it to 8/50. A
later harness-only revision reduces parser-error turns from 35 to 23 but
solves nine tasks. GPT-6-Astra selects the recovery-trained model with
the earlier harness, separating local parser feedback from task-success
feedback.

The cases below use the same decision format. Ellipses indicate omitted
designs; subset evaluations are labeled and retain their actual
graded-task denominators.

Qwen-3.8-Max tests whether the same token budget is better spent on

GPT-5.6-Sol combines a stopping rule with later data and training

With model weights fixed, adding the stopping rule increases the number
of validation tasks solved from seven to eight out of 30, while median
API calls decrease from 163 to 96.5. GPT-5.6-Sol retains the guard and

The 5,000-record model solves 52/150 tasks. Added minimal-edit, testing,
and diff-review instructions leave that total unchanged, but only 37
successes overlap: each run has 15 unique successes. A later model
trained on the complete 8,082-record pool with the original harness
solves 50/150. GLM-5.2 selects the 5,000-record model with the original

## Appendix C Additional Experimental Details

### C.1 Research-Agent Setup and Resource Accounting

Each research-agent configuration is evaluated in a separate run on each
of the five benchmark tasks. A run therefore consists of one researcher
LLM–coding-framework configuration working on one task; comparisons
concern these end-to-end configurations. Each run has access to eight
NVIDIA A100 GPUs under the task-specific wall-clock budget in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Benchmark Suite ‣ 3 VibeTraining-Bench ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement").
The clock starts when the research agent is launched and stops when the
budget expires or the research agent ends the run. Within that interval,
the research agent decides how to allocate time between training and
validation, including when to stop training and request an evaluation.
We define run duration as the elapsed time from launch to termination.
The Hours column in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
sums this duration across the five task runs, while Average is the
arithmetic mean of their five test scores.

### C.2 Initial Training Data

For each benchmark, all research-agent configurations receive the same
publicly released training resources listed in
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ C.1 Research-Agent Setup and Resource Accounting ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Details ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement").
These datasets accompany research papers or technical blogs that
document their provenance and, where reported, describe overlap checks
against the corresponding benchmark test sets used in our evaluation.
The resources form the initial editable data pool $`D_{0}`$, rather than
a prescribed training set. Research agents may select, filter, reweight,
and transform the provided resources or construct additional examples
from permitted workspace materials. The protocol prohibits using
validation tasks or grader-returned trajectories to construct $`D_{t}`$.
Research agents may use validation feedback for diagnosis, but cannot
retrieve external data during the research run.

### C.3 Task Partitions and Evaluation Protocol

For SWE-bench Verified, we randomly partition the 500 tasks into 150
validation tasks and 350 test tasks. For $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench, we randomly
partition 375 tasks into 35 validation tasks and 340 test tasks. Each
partition is sampled once and held fixed across all research-agent
configurations. Terminal-Bench 2.1 uses OpenThoughts-TBLite ¹¹ 1
[https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-thoughts/OpenThoughts-TBLite](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-thoughts/OpenThoughts-TBLite)
for validation, while Toolathlon uses ToolGym ²² 2
[https://huggingface.co/ToolGym/datasets](https://huggingface.co/ToolGym/datasets),
and AIME uses AIME 2025; their corresponding hidden tests are
Terminal-Bench 2.1, Toolathlon, and AIME 2026. There is no fixed cap on
validation requests; evaluation time counts toward the task’s research
budget. The grader returns the aggregate score, the number of graded
tasks used as its denominator, and per-task scores and output
trajectories.

Within each benchmark, validation and test evaluations use the same
decoding settings, agent-turn and token limits, and rules for timeouts
and execution failures. Timeouts and execution failures receive a score
of zero. Final evaluation covers all tasks in the test partition, and we
retain per-task scores, execution status, and grading receipts for post
hoc analysis. For benchmarks evaluated once per task, the reported score
is the fraction of test tasks completed successfully. Toolathlon uses
pass@3: each task is attempted three times and is counted as successful
if any attempt succeeds. AIME reports mean accuracy across four runs per
problem (average@4), with all four attempts included in the denominator.

## Appendix D Episode-Based Wall-Clock Attribution

Figures [17](#A4.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Appendix D Episode-Based Wall-Clock Attribution ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")–[21](#A4.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ Appendix D Episode-Based Wall-Clock Attribution ‣ VibeTraining-Bench: Data–Trainer–Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement")
summarize how research agents allocate elapsed research time across the
five benchmarks. We use episode to refer to a segment of the research
activity log associated with an activity such as data preparation,
training, or evaluation. The time breakdowns group these episodes by
activity category. waiting records episodes spent waiting for
agent-initiated training runs, while submit+grade records evaluation
submission and grading episodes. Together, these categories account for
35–95 % of elapsed time across runs with available time breakdowns. The
remaining time covers data preparation, editing, diagnostic work, and
intervals not covered by the episode records. An episode that combines
training with another activity is assigned to that other activity.
Consequently, waiting provides a lower bound on training time rather
than a complete estimate. The uncovered category records intervals
between episodes that are not assigned to any recorded activity.

Figure 17: Elapsed research time by activity for six research-agent runs
on Toolathlon, with one bar per run. waiting and submit+grade together
account for 66 % of the GPT-6-Astra run and 88 % of the Kimi-K3 run. For
GLM-5.2, a one-hour gap in the episode records leaves 9.0 % of elapsed
time classified as uncovered.

Figure 18: Elapsed research time by activity for six research-agent runs
on AIME. waiting and submit+grade together account for 76–91 % of
elapsed time across the six runs. Evaluation episodes include
submissions of individual model checkpoints or weight-averaged models on
either the full question set or a prefix selected by the limit
parameter. These episodes are classified as submit+grade. The uncovered
share never exceeds 0.6 %.

Figure 19: Elapsed research time by activity for six research-agent runs
on $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench. waiting and submit+grade together account for
69–92 % of elapsed time across the six runs. Some candidates are
constructed by interpolating the weights of existing models without
additional training. Their evaluation episodes are classified as
submit+grade.

Figure 20: Elapsed research time by activity for six research-agent runs
on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The DeepSeek-V4-Pro episode records contain
qualitative markers such as “session open”, “first full split”, “mid”,
and “last”, but no durations. Its row is retained with an explanation,
without a time breakdown. Across the five plotted runs, waiting and
submit+grade together account for 35–95 % of elapsed time. GPT-6-Astra
has the lowest combined share, with 36 % of its elapsed time classified
as uncovered.

Figure 21: Elapsed research time by activity for six research-agent runs
on SWE-bench Verified. The GPT-6-Astra episode records specify episode
order but contain only one timestamp, so its row is shown without a time
breakdown. Each episode in the other five runs has both a start and an
end timestamp; no episode duration is interpolated. Across these five
runs, waiting and submit+grade together account for 63–88 % of elapsed
time.

## Appendix E Research-Agent Prompt Template

The box below presents the shared prompt template, rather than the fully
instantiated prompt for any individual run. Before each run, the
placeholders for the benchmark, base model, GPU information, time
budget, and other task-specific setup are filled with their
corresponding values. Text enclosed by {#harness} and {/harness} is
included only for tasks with an editable inference harness. The files
referenced in the template provide additional run-specific instructions
and resources.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are the Research Agent for this {benchmark} task.

\## Objective

Improve the supplied base model ‘{model}‘’s transferable capability on
{benchmark}{#harness}

and its matching editable ‘harness/‘{/harness}. This is a

training-and-validation experiment, not an attempt to solve validation
tasks. The

development validation set is distinct from the final evaluation set and
must never

become training data.

\## Start here

Read ‘environment.md‘ first for this run’s facts. Then read

‘train_resource_manifest.lock.json‘ before changing or running anything.

Keep processes in the foreground and reserve time for checkpoint
conversion,

validation, and writing ‘final_model/‘.

\## Data

‘train_resource_manifest.lock.json‘ is the complete list of allowed
training

resources; inspect each resource and its format documentation before
using it. You may

filter, deduplicate, rebalance, mix, rewrite, augment, synthesize, or
distill

manifest-authorized data – including synthetic tasks and multi-turn
trajectories

produced with the supplied base model locally – as long as every derived
record’s

provenance traces back to manifest resources.

\## Training

The training entrypoint is named by ‘entrypoint_hint‘ in the manifest,
e.g.:

“‘bash

bash train_resources/scripts/slime_sft/run_train.sh

“‘

It reads the manifest, applies the selected recipe’s ‘env_defaults‘
unless you

override them, resolves the local base-model resource, trains, converts
the latest

complete checkpoint, and writes a loadable Hugging Face deliverable to
‘final_model/‘.

The writable framework copies under ‘framework_src/‘ (slime,
Megatron-LM) are

auto-imported by the training driver and Ray workers: you may edit their
Python or

shell code to change the algorithm, data processing, or checkpoint
handling. Compiled

CUDA/C++ changes require rebuilding the corresponding extension or
image. Set

‘TRAIN_DATA‘ explicitly whenever more than one JSONL input is available.

\## Experiment loop

Use the baseline materials and each round of validation feedback to form
and test the

next transferable hypothesis. Iteratively improve model capability
through

manifest-authorized data, training changes{#harness}, or general harness
behavior{/harness}.

‘agent_rules.md‘ defines the integrity boundary{#harness}; ‘harness.md‘
defines the

harness contract{/harness}.

If this benchmark declares a validation context pack (the manifest’s

‘validation_context‘), inspect its baseline analysis and the initial
trajectories

before choosing the first experiment. Separate clean model failures from

infrastructure errors and missing trajectories. Do not convert
validation material

into training records, prompts, rules, or task-specific heuristics.

For every validation submission, create a candidate snapshot and submit
it through

‘grading.md‘ as ‘environment.md‘ (## Candidates) describes. Each
completed validation

returns a trajectory archive under ‘\$HOME/grading_results/\<job_id\>/‘;
use it only for

diagnosis.

\## Final delivery

Select the completed candidate{#harness} – a model-and-harness pair
–{/harness} using

its candidate record and validation evidence; ‘environment.md‘ (##
Candidates) states

the snapshot and submission procedure, and ‘agent_rules.md‘ states the
delivery rules.

Keep all submitted candidate directories in place.

{gpu_info}

Time budget: ‘{num_hours}‘ hours; ‘bash timer.sh‘ reports what is left.

{setup_other}
````
